tier_reason: The orjson README (shipped unchanged in orjson 3.9.4, measured with orjson 3.7.9 and ujson 5.4.0 on Python 3.10.5) is an independent, widely cited third-party comparison with public harness code (bench/benchmark_dumps.py, bench/benchmark_loads.py, bench/util.py, script/pybench: pytest-benchmark, GC disabled, CPUs 0-1 pinned) and has ujson and stdlib json rows. Every latency in the record matches. It falls short of A because no CPU model is given and the ujson wheel's compiler and flags are not stated. UltraJSON's own README table (tests/benchmark.py, Azure VM, no CPU model) is first-party and would be C on its own.

corrections.claimed_speedup: orjson README Performance tables (unchanged in 3.9.4; measured with orjson 3.7.9, ujson 5.4.0, Python 3.10.5, Linux amd64), median latency ujson vs stdlib json, ratios derived from page data: canada.json serialize 14.16 vs 35.7 ms (2.5x faster), deserialize 8.73 vs 21.1 ms (2.4x); citm_catalog.json serialize 2.89 vs 3.93 ms (1.4x), deserialize 3.5 vs 4.99 ms (1.4x); twitter.json serialize 1.68 vs 1.8 ms (1.07x), deserialize 1.87 vs 2.45 ms (1.3x); github.json serialize 0.18 vs 0.18 ms (tie), deserialize 0.19 vs 0.16 ms (ujson slower). The same README's pretty-print rows (derived from page data) show the largest gaps, because json's indent path is pure Python: github.json pretty 0.19 vs 0.71 ms (3.7x) and citm_catalog.json pretty 3.59 vs 33.42 ms (9.3x). Sorted twitter.json is 2.07 vs 2.32 ms (1.1x).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: orjson README: Python 3.10.5 on Linux (amd64) with the ujson 5.4.0 PyPI wheel; the wheel's compiler and flags are not stated. ujson's setup.py adds only -D_GNU_SOURCE (optimization comes from CPython's sysconfig defaults), compiles the bundled C++ double-conversion library plus dconv_wrapper.cc, and links -lstdc++ -lm; wheels are built in CI with cibuildwheel. UltraJSON's own README table used CPython 3.11.3 built with GCC 11.3.0 and ujson 5.7.1.dev26.
corrections.caveats: Python-only since 6.0.0: commit 'Collapse the /lib vs /python source code split' (2026-07-26, released 2026-09-04) removed the JSONObjectDecoder callback struct and replaced JSOBJ with PyObject*. src/ujson/encode.c and decode.c now include Python.h and build Python objects directly, so the current code is not a C library callable from C or C++ without embedding CPython. Up to 5.13.0, src/ujson/lib/ (ultrajsondec.c, ultrajsonenc.c, ultrajson.h) was a Python-free callback API (JSON_DecodeObject, JSON_EncodeObject); its decoder is what esnme/ujson4c wraps, and ujson4c is already listed (wave 4, tier A, nativejson-benchmark). All UltraJSON numbers are Python-level, against CPython's json module, whose _json C accelerator does the scanning and compact encoding, so the baseline is itself largely C. The baseline is not a C++ library, and the guessed list (nlohmann/json) does not apply. The win is workload-dependent and small on modern CPython: a tie on github.json serialize and slower on github.json deserialize. In UltraJSON's own README, decoding an array of 256 strings (28,518 vs 42,221 calls/s) and encoding 256 UTF-8 strings (3,457 vs 3,653) are slower than json, and ujson trails orjson everywhere (256 doubles encode 18,282 vs 79,569). The independent numbers are from 2022 (ujson 5.4.0); the first-party ones are from 2023 (5.7.1.dev26). The README puts the project in maintenance-only mode: 'UltraJSON's architecture is fundamentally ill-suited to making changes without risk of introducing new security vulnerabilities'. It recommends migrating to orjson. Security advisories: double free and surrogate mishandling (fixed in 5.4.0); an integer overflow on a large indent leading to buffer overflow or an infinite loop, and a memory leak parsing large integers (both fixed in 5.12.0); a ujson.dump() leak on write failure (5.12.1); malformed UTF-8 accepted in dumps of bytes (5.13.0); loose continuation-byte validation in loads from bytes (#750, 6.0.0). The #750 fix changes a mask from 0x80 to 0xc0 and adds error cases, so it does not alter valid-input speed. The orjson README also reports that ujson segfaulted on sorting int keys, fails to reject 38 of 342 invalid JSONTestSuite/nativejson documents (json: 17), and returns '' for a lone surrogate escape. The nativejson-benchmark figures (parse of 3 files 8.95 ms vs Nlohmann 72.48 ms, derived from the i7-4980HQ clang 7.0 CSV; Parse Double 34/66 and Parse String 5/9 correct) belong to ujson4c, not to this package. License terms: EA BSD-3-Clause, plus the modp_ascii BSD notice and permissive TCL terms for the numeric decoder; the bundled double-conversion is BSD-3-Clause. No patent grant.

notes: All claimed numbers match the orjson README tables and UltraJSON's own README, and metadata checks out (4.5k stars, not a fork, not archived, last commit 2026-10-05, latest release 6.0.0 on 2026-09-04); PyPI declares the license as 'BSD-3-Clause AND TCL', and the language field could read 'C (CPython extension; bundled C++ double-conversion)'. On the C++ question: UltraJSON does NOT qualify as a C library callable from C++. Since 6.0.0 its encoder and decoder are fused with the CPython API, and its measured claims are Python-level against stdlib json. Keep it only as a Python-binding entry on the same footing as orjson and ssrJSON in wave 4 json, flagged 'Python-only, not usable from C++'. It is not a cross-language claim, since both sides are C. C++ users wanting its decoder core already have esnme/ujson4c (listed, tier A), so this is not a duplicate of ujson4c: the claims and baselines differ.
